contributions: An information-theoretic framing of experience extraction as retaining what predicts future competence while discarding instance-specific detail, used to place test-time and training-time self-evolution as two approximations of the same extractor
A global experience pool that is evolved rather than accumulated: an operator merges overlapping items, resolves conflicts and abstracts trajectory-specific observations away

A measured acceptance test — each candidate item's marginal utility is the change in expected reward on a held-out probe set when it is added to the pool, screened cheaply on a subset first and then on the full probe set

Internalization by on-policy self-distillation from a teacher branch that sees the pool as privileged context, rather than by distilling reference trajectories, which the paper argues is what avoids teaching post-hoc rationalization of specific answers

Evidence that the point of the pre-stage is exploration quality rather than accuracy directly: it lowers the share of problems where every sampled response is wrong, which is exactly the case where group-relative advantages are uninformative
limitations: The conclusion's stated limitation is really future work — extending to domains with sparser or less reliable feedback. What a reader should weigh instead: the margin over GRPO is 0.75 to 1.92 average points with no seeds, variance or repeated runs reported anywhere, on five benchmarks two of which (AIME24/25 at 1.7B, at 5.21 and 7.71) are small enough that the average is carried by GSM8K and MATH500. The efficiency claim counts training trajectories and steps but not the extra forward passes spent extracting items, running the evolution operator, and scoring marginal utility on a probe set — so 28% fewer trajectories is not 28% less compute, and no wall-clock or FLOP accounting is given for Stage I. The main experiments use a single evolution round while the iteration study shows sampling accuracy still climbing at four, so the reported configuration is explicitly not the converged one. The extractor is the model being trained, which bounds experience quality by the current policy; the paper calls the items provisional hypotheses and filters them by utility, but never measures how often a wrong or misleading item survives the filter, nor what the acceptance threshold rejects. Everything is mathematics on one base-model family.
method: For each problem the current policy samples G responses, each scored by a binary reward and partitioned into successful and failed sets; a subset is drawn preserving the empirical success proportion, and the same model acting as extractor converts each selected trajectory into an experience item — effective patterns from successes, recurring failure modes from failures. New items are merged into a provisional pool by an evolution operator, then each is kept only if its marginal utility on a held-out probe set exceeds a threshold. The refined pool is then internalized: a teacher branch receives the problem plus the global experience and a student branch receives the problem alone, both sharing parameters with the teacher detached; the student samples on-policy, the teacher rescores those tokens under the experience-augmented condition, and the student minimizes the reverse KL to that target. Stage II runs standard GRPO on the resulting policy. Training uses DAPO-math-17k on Qwen3-1.7b, 4b and 8b base models, with the number of training steps and total sampled rollouts controlled across methods; evaluation is pass@16 average on AIME24 and AIME25 and pass@1 on GSM8K, MATH500 and Minerva Math, against the base checkpoint, a hand-written domain prompt, GRPO, and a self-distillation baseline.
one_liner: Inserts a stage before RL in which the model extracts textual lessons from its own successful and failed rollouts, filters them by measured marginal utility on a held-out probe set, and distills the surviving pool into its own weights — so that GRPO starts from a policy that fails all-eight-samples less often.
problem: Self-evolution splits into two families that do not meet. Test-time methods keep demonstrations, reflections or retrieved notes as extra context, so the knowledge stays outside the parameters and is bounded by context capacity and retrieval quality. Training-time RL writes behaviour into the parameters but absorbs experience only through a scalar reward, so when sampled trajectories are mostly wrong the supervision carries almost no information about what to do instead. The missing stage is turning transient interaction into transferable text and then into parameters, before reward-driven exploration begins.

relevance.reasoning-evaluation: Its transferable contribution to evaluation is the intermediate quantity it reports rather than the headline average. Final accuracy separates it from GRPO by about one point, which no reader should trust without seeds; but the all-samples-incorrect rate and the sampling accuracy across evolution rounds measure something accuracy cannot — whether a policy is producing groups that carry any gradient signal at all. That is the right diagnostic for a family of methods whose failure mode is silent: when every rollout in a group shares a reward, group-relative RL trains on nothing and the loss curve does not say so. It also supplies a control worth copying — post-stage policy entropy at 0.047 against GRPO's 0.029, which rules out the cheapest explanation for an improved initialization, namely that diversity was traded away. Read against this archive's other credit-assignment papers, it is another instance of the ablation being more informative than the benchmark table: removing the experience pool costs more than removing the reinforcement-learning stage entirely.

results: Average accuracy across the five benchmarks improves over the base checkpoint by 4.87, 6.96 and 6.53 points at 1.7B, 4B and 8B, against 4.12, 5.04 and 5.74 for GRPO — a margin over GRPO of 0.75, 1.92 and 0.79 points, which the paper states as a 1.16% average improvement. The margin is not uniform per benchmark: GRPO takes Minerva at 1.7B (14.07 against 13.97) and the self-distillation baseline takes AIME25 at 4B (10.83 against 8.75). The mechanism evidence is more convincing than the headline. Stage I alone cuts the proportion of problems on which all eight sampled responses are wrong by 4.95 points at 4B and 2.75 at 8B, which is precisely the case where every response in a group shares a reward and the normalized advantage is zero, so GRPO gets no gradient. Policy entropy after Stage I stays at 0.047 against 0.029 for GRPO, so the initialization does not come from collapsing diversity. The ablation puts the pool above the RL stage in importance: at 4B, removing Stage II gives 35.16 while removing the shared experience pool gives 34.13, both below the full 36.67, and the same ordering holds at 8B (36.14 against 35.48, full 38.71). Data efficiency follows from the better start — matched performance at roughly 28% fewer training trajectories and 28.0% fewer steps, a 1.39x speedup. Iterating the evolution loop keeps paying: sampling accuracy rises 18.83, 20.55, 21.33, 21.80, 22.66 percent across zero to four rounds. The qualitative case is the clearest statement of what is being transferred — the injected experience for a digit-constraint problem contains neither the answer nor any candidate, only a decomposition procedure, and the model then enumerates exhaustively where before it had produced an incomplete candidate set.
